description: Covered porches, screened porches, and gazebos built for Middle Tennessee homes. Plan the roof, floor, and screens with us and get a free estimate.
intro: We build covered porches, screened porches, and gazebos for homeowners across Middle Tennessee. A roof turns a deck into a room you can use in July heat and April rain, and screens keep the mosquitoes on the other side. If you already have a deck, we can often build a roof over it. If you are starting from grass, we can build the floor and the roof together. Either way, the [estimate form](#estimate) is the easiest way to start.

sections.heading: Covered porches and roofs over decks
paragraphs: A covered porch is a deck or floor with a roof on posts. The roof keeps the sun off the table in the afternoon and lets you sit outside while it rains. Most of the planning happens where the new roof meets the house, because that joint has to shed water and tie in cleanly with your gutters and siding.

Roof style changes the look and the cost. A shed roof slopes one way and works well on a single story house or under a second story window. A gable roof rises to a peak and suits a porch that sticks out from the house. Metal roofing is common here because it sheds water fast and holds up to storms, and shingles can be matched to the house when the neighborhood calls for it. A wood ceiling under the roof finishes the space and gives you a place for a ceiling fan and lights.

sections.heading: Screened porches for Tennessee summers
paragraphs: A screened porch is a covered porch with screen walls and a screen door. In Middle Tennessee it is often the room people use most from spring through fall, because it keeps out mosquitoes, flies, and falling leaves while letting the breeze through. Screen panels come in different strengths, and pet resistant screen is worth considering if a dog will lean on it.

The bottom of the walls matters as much as the screen. A short knee wall or a railing along the bottom protects the screen from chairs and paws, and it gives the room a finished look. The floor can be deck boards with a screen layer underneath to keep bugs from coming up through the gaps. The screen door should swing out toward the yard and close on its own.

sections.heading: Gazebos and freestanding roofs
paragraphs: A gazebo or pavilion is a roof on posts that stands on its own, away from the house. It works over a patio, beside a pool, or at the end of a path in the yard. Because it does not attach to the house, it is often simpler to build, but the posts still need solid footings so the roof stays square through wind and storms.

Think about where the shade lands at the time of day you use the space. A gazebo in the right spot can cover an outdoor kitchen, a hot tub, or a table for eight. Wood posts with metal roofing and knee braces give a sturdy look that fits most Tennessee yards. If the gazebo sits on grass rather than a patio, we can build a deck floor under it so the space stays dry and level.

sections.heading: What a porch or roof needs before we build
paragraphs: Most attached porches and roofs need a building permit, and many subdivisions need HOA approval first. Rules differ between cities and counties, so check with the codes office for your address before the design is final. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a deck or fence](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) covers the same kind of submission a porch needs.

An existing deck has to be checked before a roof goes on it. A roof adds weight and wind load, so the posts, beams, and footings under the deck may need to be added to or rebuilt. If the deck is worn, our guide on [whether to repair or replace a deck](/guides/signs-you-need-a-new-deck/) explains what we look for.

sections.heading: Porches, decks, and fences together
paragraphs: Many projects mix all three. A covered section next to an open deck gives you shade and sun in one space. Stairs from a porch should land near a gate if the yard is fenced. Planning them together keeps the materials and colors matched and means one permit and one HOA request instead of several. See our [deck building page](/decks/) and [fence page](/fences/) for the rest of what we build.

faqs.q: Can you put a roof over the deck I already have?
faqs.a: Often, yes. We check the posts, beams, footings, and the connection to the house first, since a roof adds weight and catches wind. Some decks only need added posts and footings. Others are worn enough that rebuilding the floor with the roof makes more sense. We tell you which one we see before you decide.

faqs.q: Do you build screened porches from scratch?
faqs.a: Yes. We can build the floor, the roof, and the screen walls as one project, or add screens to a covered porch you already have. The floor can be raised like a deck or built lower to the ground, depending on the house and the yard.

faqs.q: Do you build gazebos and pavilions?
faqs.a: Yes. We build freestanding gazebos and pavilions over patios, pools, and seating areas. Tell us what you want to cover and where it sits in the yard, and we will plan the size, the roof, and the footings around it.

faqs.q: Is the estimate for a porch free?
faqs.a: Yes. Estimates are free for porches, decks, fences, and repairs. Use the form below to tell us about the project and send a few photos of the spot if you have them. We will follow up to set a time to look at the house and the yard, then give you the price in writing.
